newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dutch transport minister faces difficult presidency.
newsitem.headline: Dutch transport minister faces difficult presidency.

text.p: Dutch transport and public works minister Annemarie Jorritsma made clear on Thursday she would be wearing two conflicting hats during her six-month term as president of the European Union Transport Council.

Jorritsma, who is responsible until June for brokering agreements between the 15 EU countries on transport and related questions, indicated to the European Parliament's transport committee that her own country, the Netherlands, was deeply at odds with other member states on at least two counts.

She said the Netherlands was "disappointed" with EU ministers' recent agreement in principle to partially liberalise postal services, accusing them of lacking the political will to really open up the sector to competition.

The comments raised the eyebrows of the parliament's rapporteur on the draft postal services directive, British Socialist Brian Simpson, who asked for assurances that Jorritsma would respect the ministers' deal and strive to finalise it.
The Dutch minister said the Netherlands was also unhappy with the European Commission's proposal, currently being discussed by ministers, to revise the EU's existing "Eurovignette" tax system.

She said she viewed as merely "provisional measures" the revised Eurovignette rules, COM(96)331, which would favour cleaner trucks with low axle weights over dirtier trucks carrying the higher axle loads that cause greatest damage to roads and bridges.

Jorritsma told MEPs she hoped progress could be made during the Dutch presidency on a whole string of legislative proposals which Ireland tackled during its leadership of the Council in the last six months of 1996.
But she added that many of the proposals were controversial and few were likely to reach the statute books before the Hague hands over the reins to Luxembourg on June 30.

"Difficult" dossiers that would need attention included proposals for an EU-wide air traffic control system, excise duty on aeroplane fuel, expanding trans-European road and rail networks and a deal with Switzerland to resolve trans-Alpine freight traffic problems related to a Swiss ban on heavy trucks.

Jorritsma said a deal with the Swiss would have to calm their fears of a huge increase in lorries transiting its territory but resist their attempts to impose such punitive levies on traffic that heavy trucks chose en masse to use Austrian and French roads instead.
The Dutch minister said she would commission a study on the merits of introducing excise duties on kerosene, which is exempt from the EU-wide levy on mineral oils under directive 92/81.
She denied suggestions from MEPs that calling for a study was just a delaying tactic, saying it might help debunk arguments against the tax which she personally found dubious.
"I find it intellectually odd that you can have taxes on some fuels but not on kerosene," she said.

Jorritsma was more optimistic about concluding Council discussions on a draft regulation, COM(94)323, amending the existing directive and regulation on recording equipment in road transport (tachographs).
She also hoped to achieve by July a final decision on standard EU dates for summertime arrangements and an extension of a scheme to promote combined transport systems (PACT).
But she said the Dutch presidency has "no spectacular plans" to achieve a breakthrough in talks with the U.S. on aviation relations or in Council discussions on several files on maritime transport.
Work on several air safety dossiers of concern to MEPs would have to wait until the Commission had drafted specific proposals, Jorritsma said.

The transport committee is concerned about the proposed merger of giants British Airways and American Airlines, mainly because of the effect that pooling deals like this could have on slot allocations at congested airports.
